source.title: The Missing Curve Detectors of InceptionV1: Applying Sparse Autoencoders to InceptionV1 Early Vision

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. An unresolved “??” cross-reference appears in the text but does not prevent reading the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: The paper applies sparse autoencoders to InceptionV1 neurons and examines whether neurons described as polysemantic can be decomposed into more interpretable features, using a different method from neuron-based analysis.
record.gate_note: The paper reports qualitative results for specific neuron decompositions, recorded below. It also reports new SAE curve-detector features filling gaps in neuron coverage, but those are feature findings rather than results about individual neurons. It does not systematically estimate the prevalence of polysemantic neurons.
record.test_reason: The study uses sparse autoencoders, a different method from neuron inspection, on InceptionV1 early vision. It reports how specific neurons considered polysemantic decompose into features. This bears on V1 (do vision neurons mix several features) and V6 (do apparent mixtures reduce to one shared or related feature). The evidence is qualitative and drawn from selected examples.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that SAEs reveal interpretable features not visible from neurons, including missing curve detectors, and split some polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic features. They see SAEs as promising for InceptionV1 and CNNs.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses sparse autoencoders trained on InceptionV1 image activations, then analyzes SAE features with dataset examples and feature visualizations; it is not a reproduction of neuron-based analysis. It also uses synthetic curve stimuli for curve-detector analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: For mixed3b/n/359, higher SAE L1 coefficients reduce the maximum activation of analogous double-curve features while increasing the maxima of left- and right-curve features.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE features include curve detectors at orientations no InceptionV1 neuron covers, filling gaps in the curve neuron family (Fig. 2). The appendix shows many mixed3b features spread across branches.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vision CNNs represent interpretable features that align with no single neuron and are distributed across neurons.

record.problems: The authors call this a very early report and say they do not aim to defend the representativeness of their examples systematically. Evidence about neuron decomposition is qualitative and based on selected examples. The paper also notes that its branch-specific SAEs may miss cross-branch superposition.
record.rows_left_out: No additional neuron-decomposition results bearing on the claim were reported. New curve-detector features that fill gaps are feature-level results, not findings about individual neurons, and are therefore not recorded as rows.

untested.parts: Prevalence of polysemantic neurons; later layers and the named cat/car neuron; other vision models.
All parts; no language models are studied.
Causal role of capacity pressure. The SAE decomposition is interpreted as superposition but not tested as the cause.
All parts; no architecture or training comparison of neuron polysemanticity.
How rare truly unrelated mixtures are across neurons.
Effect of activation range or explanation scoring on neuron classification.

missing.what: Five interpretable SAE features, one per early-vision layer, whose most-involved neurons are described as vaguely related or polysemantic. This is qualitative evidence for V1 across layers.

record.verdict_notes: This is an early, self-described non-systematic report from a single author. The polysemantic status of the neurons is largely taken from Olah et al. 2020. The branch-specific SAEs may miss cross-branch superposition, as the appendix acknowledges. No original source of the claim is involved.

versions.untested_parts: The paper studies selected early-vision neurons in InceptionV1, not the named 4e:55 neuron or the prevalence of mixed responses across vision models.
Language models and the share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by having more sparse features than neurons and packing features together; the paper does not test capacity pressure.
Polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise when there are enough neurons.

The share of polysemantic neurons across architectures, activation functions, or regularization settings, and performance costs. The paper varies SAE L1 coefficients but does not measure those outcomes.
The prevalence of genuinely unrelated mixtures across neurons; the paper presents selected examples, not a systematic frequency estimate.
Whether polysemanticity classification changes with the activation range examined or with explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Applied an SAE and examined the features representing conv2d1/n/44.
rows.measure: Qualitative description of features into which the neuron was decomposed
rows.value: The SAE decomposed the neuron into features responding to brightness gradients of various orientations, colour contrast, and complex Gabor filters.
rows.note: The paper describes the neuron as previously difficult to categorize and polysemantic. The reported feature types are qualitatively diverse; no prevalence or quantitative response-strength measure is given.
rows.check: Observed for V1: the neuron splits into gradients, colour contrast and Gabor features. For V6 the state is effectively absent, because the better tool reveals a mixture rather than one shared feature. All the features are low-level, so how unrelated they are is arguable. The 'previously uncategorizable' status is cited from Olah et al. 2020.

source_check.problem: none. 'Observed' fits V1 because the text says the neuron 'appears quite polysemantic'. The verdict fix records the V6 state as absent.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Applied an SAE and examined the features representing mixed3b/n/376.
rows.measure: Qualitative description of features into which the neuron was decomposed
rows.value: The neuron was decomposed into a generic boundary detector and a fur-specific boundary detector in the same orientation.
rows.note: The paper presents these as related boundary features, rather than unrelated jobs.
rows.check: The authors describe this neuron as relatively monosemantic, not polysemantic. The split into a generic boundary feature and a fur boundary feature is a related-offshoot pattern, consistent with V6. It does not bear on V1.

source_check.correct: For V6 the state should be cannot_determine, or the row should be unlinked (versions none). The text lists n/376 among the 'more monosemantic corresponding neurons'. It responds to boundaries with a preference for fur on one side. The SAE splits it into a generic and a fur-specific boundary detector in the same orientation.
source_check.problem: The text does not present the neuron as polysemantic, so its split cannot show V6's effect (a polysemantic neuron that turns out to be related offshoots).

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Applied an SAE and examined the features representing the double-curve neuron.
rows.measure: Qualitative decomposition of the double-curve detector
rows.value: The neuron primarily decomposed into three features: two monosemantic curve detectors and a double-curve detector.
rows.note: The two curve features correspond to different orientations, but the SAE also retains a double-curve feature.
rows.check: For V1 the state is observed: the neuron responds to curves in two very different orientations and splits into two single-curve features, though the two inputs are related (both curves). For V6 it is partial: a residual double-curve feature persists, so a shared feature is not fully ruled out.

source_check.correct: The state is partial for V1 too, as the row's own state says, not observed as the verdict fix says. The neuron responds to 'curves in two very different orientations', which are related inputs. The SAE primarily gives two monosemantic curve detectors plus a double-curve detector.
source_check.problem: The verdict fix raises the V1 state to observed, though it admits both inputs are curves and the double-curve feature remains.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Compared analogous SAE features for the double-curve neuron across higher L1 coefficients.

conditions.value: two higher coefficients; values not stated

rows.measure: Maximum activations of analogous double-curve and single-curve SAE features
rows.note: The text says the double-curve feature's maximum activation falls as L1 increases, while the left- and right-curve feature maxima increase. Exact plotted values and the higher L1 coefficients are not stated.
rows.check: As the L1 coefficient rises, the putative shared double-curve feature weakens and the single-curve features grow. This points to a mixture rather than one shared feature. The values are in a figure only and the L1 coefficients are not stated. The result also shows the decomposition depends on the SAE's L1 setting.

source_check.correct: Text: two additional SAEs with higher L1. As L1 rises, the double-curve feature's maximum activation falls and the left and right curve maxima grow. No L1 values or numbers are stated (Figure 3 bottom).

relationships.reason: The SAE splits each of these neurons into several distinct features: gradients, colour and Gabor features for n/44, and opposite-orientation curves for n/359 (r1, r3). Their polysemantic status is partly drawn from prior work.
relationships.display_finding: A sparse autoencoder split conv2d1/n/44 into gradient, colour and Gabor features, and split mixed3b/n/359 into curves of opposite orientation. Part of the case that these neurons are polysemantic comes from prior work.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: n/44 'appears quite polysemantic' and splits into gradient, colour-contrast and Gabor features (r1, observed). n/359 is a 'likely polysemantic' double-curve detector (r3, partial, both inputs curves).

relationships.reason: The neuron decomposes into a generic boundary detector and a fur-specific boundary detector, which are related offshoots of one job (r2).
relationships.display_finding: This neuron decomposes into a generic boundary detector and a fur-specific boundary detector, two related offshoots of one job. The paper itself presents it as a more monosemantic neuron, a boundary detector with a fur preference, not as a polysemantic one.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: The text presents n/376 as a more monosemantic neuron (boundaries with a fur preference). Its split into related boundary features does not test whether polysemantic neurons turn out to be one feature or related offshoots.

relationships.reason: Better tools reveal mixtures of distinct features rather than one shared feature (r1, r3). For n/359, the double-curve feature shrinks as L1 rises (r4). The features stay within low-level families, so this is not a clear challenge.
relationships.display_finding: Better tools reveal mixtures of distinct features in these neurons rather than one shared feature, and for n/359 the double-curve feature shrinks as the L1 penalty rises. The features still stay within low-level families.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: The SAE shows mixtures of distinct low-level features rather than one shared feature (r1, r3), and the double-curve feature weakens at higher L1 (r4). The features are not clearly unrelated, so this is a limit, not a challenge.

tranche.reason: SAE features with dataset examples are a different method aimed at the same question about InceptionV1 neurons.

source_check.notes: This is a short single-author preprint that calls itself a 'very early report'. It is qualitative, uses hand-picked neurons and gives no counts. The mixed3a and mixed3b SAEs were trained on one branch only (3x3 and 5x5). Appendix A says cross-branch superposition is larger than expected. The extracted text is complete but its two columns are out of order.

statements.correction: n/359 (L1 3.5e-6, 8x) responds to curves in two very different orientations. It primarily decomposes into two monosemantic curve detectors and a double-curve detector (Figure 3), state partial. n/44 (L1 5e-6, 4x) splits into brightness-gradient, colour-contrast and complex Gabor features. The model is InceptionV1 via Lucent's PyTorch port with the local response normalisation fixed. The SAEs are trained on ILSVRC activations.
statements.problem: Calls n/359 observed for V1 and says it splits into curves of opposite orientations. It leaves out the third, double-curve feature, and the two inputs are related curves, so the row's state (partial) fits better. The model note 'PyTorch with batch norm' sits beside this study's conditions, but this study uses Lucent's port with fixes to local response normalisation.

statements.correction: The study does not examine 4e:55. It mentions mixed4e only in a preliminary branch-specialisation SAE (Appendix A).
The study covers early-vision layers conv2d0 to mixed3b. It is qualitative and gives no count of polysemantic units.
For this study: early-vision neurons the author calls polysemantic split into several SAE features. The results are qualitative, from selected examples, in a 'very early report'.

n/376 responds to boundaries with a fur preference and is listed among 'more monosemantic corresponding neurons'. The SAE (L1 3.5e-6, 8x, 5x5-branch SAE) splits it into a generic and a fur-specific boundary detector in the same orientation. V6 verdict for this neuron: none.
statements.problem: The decomposition and settings are right, and the caveat is disclosed. But the text presents n/376 as a more monosemantic neuron, not a polysemantic one, so it does not test V6 and should not be listed as support.

statements.correction: n/44 gives gradient, colour-contrast and complex Gabor features. n/359 primarily gives three features. At two higher, unstated L1 values the double-curve maximum falls and the single-curve maxima rise (Figure 3 bottom).
No random-sample rate. The neurons are hand-picked.
n/376 is listed among 'more monosemantic corresponding neurons', so it does not test V6 (verdict none). This study's only V6 verdict is limits_scope, from n/44 and n/359.
statements.problem: It is right that the authors present n/376 as relatively monosemantic. For that reason it does not test V6, so calling it 'the InceptionV1 neuron that supports the version' is wrong.

statements.correction: With the same SAE method, n/376 gives related boundary features and n/44 and n/359 give distinct features. Note that n/376 was not called polysemantic.
n/376 splits into a generic and a fur-specific boundary detector, so the common job is boundary detection.

n/44 splits into brightness gradients of various orientations, colour contrast and complex Gabor filters, several low-level feature types. n/359 splits into two curve detectors plus a double-curve detector. The study states no criterion for relatedness.
statements.problem: 'Within one low-level family' fits n/359 (all curves) but not n/44. The text describes n/44's features as 'a variety' of three different low-level types.

statements.correction: At two higher, unstated L1 coefficients the analogous double-curve feature's maximum activation falls and the left and right curve features' maxima rise (Figure 3 bottom). The feature weakens but does not vanish. The authors ran this to test whether the double-curve feature was an SAE failure.
statements.problem: The trend is right, but 'whether a shared double-curve feature appears' overreads it. The text says the feature 'becomes smaller', and analogous features exist at every L1 tried.

statements.correction: With the same tool the study finds related offshoots for n/376 and distinct features for n/44 and n/359. If l1 becomes none, this study no longer counts among V6 'supports' studies.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The SAE analyses identify multiple feature responses for the described neurons, including diverse feature types for conv2d1/n/44 and differently oriented curves for mixed3b/n/359 (r1, r3).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The decompositions include related boundary variants and two individual curve detectors, consistent with some apparent mixtures separating into related features (r2, r3).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The conv2d1 neuron decomposes into several qualitatively different feature types, and the double-curve feature for mixed3b/n/359 remains present, although its maximum activation falls at higher L1 (r1, r3, r4). The selected examples do not establish how common either pattern is.
